Choosing stimuli is a constrained selection problem. One lexical property is
manipulated, several others must not vary with it, and the words that satisfy
every constraint at once are a small and awkward subset of the language. This
vignette covers how `lexsync` states those constraints and how it resolves them:
the dimensions it computes, the filters that narrow a lexicon to a candidate
pool, the four matching methods and the situations each one suits, the tolerance
windows that bound an acceptable match, the continuous alternative to a matched
dichotomy, and the report that tells you what control the selection actually
achieved.

Everything below runs on the English example lexicon bundled with the package, a
3000-word slice that needs no download. It is cut from the screened English
lexicon. The screen leaves out the forms SUBTLEX-US lacks or writes with a capital
in more than 90% of their uses, such as proper names and acronyms. The slice's N
and OLD20 count only the forms it keeps. Taboo words and some abbreviations pass
the screen, and a lexicon of your own is taken as given.
[Choosing and screening a lexicon](#choosing-and-screening-a-lexicon) below says
what such forms do to a selection and how to screen them out.

```{r setup}
library(lexsync)
schema <- yaml::read_yaml(
  system.file("extdata", "schema.yaml", package = "lexsync")
)
lex <- load_lexicon(
  system.file("extdata", "en_example.csv", package = "lexsync"),
  schema, language = "english"
)
head(
  lex[, c("word", "frequency", "length", "n_syllables", "n_density", "old20")],
  4
)
```

## The lexical dimensions

A dimension is any numeric column the matcher can equate. `lexsync` distinguishes
those read straight from the lexicon file from those computed from the
orthographic form at load time, and the schema records the distinction along with
each dimension's unit. Units matter when reading a report: a raw difference of 1
means one letter on `length` but a factor of ten in corpus occurrence on
`frequency`, which is why the comparisons are standardised.

```{r dimensions}
dims <- schema$dimensions
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  dimension = names(dims),
  type = vapply(dims, function(d) d$type, character(1)),
  unit = vapply(dims, function(d) d$unit, character(1)),
  row.names = NULL
), caption = "The dimensions declared in schema.yaml")
```

`length` is the character count of the orthographic form. `frequency` is the Zipf
value read from the lexicon's `freq_zipf` column, a log-scaled measure on which
roughly 1 is a word occurring once per hundred million tokens and 7 a word
occurring ten thousand times per million. The value is the base-10 logarithm of
the frequency per billion words (van Heuven et al., 2014). It is
preferred to raw counts because it is linear in the log space in which frequency
effects are approximately linear, and because it is comparable across corpora of
different sizes. `n_density` is Coltheart's N, the count of same-length words
differing by one letter substitution (Coltheart et al., 1977). `old20` is the
mean Levenshtein distance to the twenty nearest words in the reference set, which
unlike Coltheart's N is defined for long words, where substitution neighbours run
out (Yarkoni et al., 2008). A larger OLD20 means a more isolated word, so it runs
in the opposite direction to `n_density`.

`n_syllables` also arrives at load time, counting maximal runs of vowels, an
orthographic estimate with no pronunciation model behind it. Only
`bigram_freq` is computed on request, by `add_bigram_frequency()`: it is the mean
corpus probability of a word's adjacent letter bigrams, standing proxy for
phonotactic probability.

```{r syllables}
count_syllables(c("cat", "table", "rhythm", "being", "chocolate"))
```

The estimate is worth its caveat, and the errors run in both directions. It
handles `rhythm` because `y` is treated as a vowel letter. It undercounts
`being`, whose `ei` is one run of vowel letters spanning two nuclei, and it
overcounts `chocolate`, whose silent final `e` forms a run of its own. The
measure is adequate for equating two conditions on gross syllabic complexity and
it is not a substitute for a pronunciation dictionary.

A vowel counts whatever its accent, since the word is decomposed and its
diacritics set aside, so the vowels of Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Romanian,
Turkish and Vietnamese count as those of English do. The estimate is defined for
Latin orthographies only: a word holding a character outside the Latin script
gets `NA`. `run_pipeline()` refuses a design that refers to `n_syllables` when
such a word passes the other filters the lexicon can answer. The reproducibility
vignette gives the exact letters and code points.

### Computing dimensions on a pool

The bundled lexicon arrives with `n_density` and `old20` already present, but
neighbourhood measures depend on the reference set they are computed against, so
a lexicon derived elsewhere may need them recomputed. `add_neighbourhood()` does
that. Both measures are quadratic in the size of the reference set, which is why
the pipeline computes them on the pool alone, and why the reference should still
be the whole lexicon: a word's neighbours are its neighbours in the language,
not among the handful of words that survived your filters.

`run_pipeline()` computes `n_density`, `old20` and `bigram_freq` for a lexicon
that lacks them whenever the design refers to them, in `match_on`, a condition's
`define_by`, `pool_filters`, a continuous predictor or control, or
`counterbalance.balance_on`. A filter on a derived dimension waits until it is
computed, after the others have shrunk the pool. A lexicon can name the words
that make up the reference with a `reference_member` column (1 for a member, 0
otherwise). The `reference_words` argument recomputes N and OLD20, and
`bigram_freq` where the lexicon carries it or the design uses it, against a list
of your own, overriding the lexicon's columns. The datasheet then records the list with the columns it
was applied to.

```{r neighbourhood}
sample_words <- lex[lex$word %in% c("apple", "boat", "dog", "rhythm"), ]
add_neighbourhood(
  sample_words, reference = lex$word
)[, c("word", "n_density", "old20")]
```

`add_bigram_frequency()` works the same way, and `merge_norms()` joins any
word-keyed norm table, which is how dimensions the corpus does not carry
(concreteness, age of acquisition, behavioural measures from a megastudy) become
matchable. Once a column is present, the matcher treats it like any other.

```{r norms}
aoa <- data.frame(word = c("apple", "boat", "dog"), aoa = c(3.1, 3.0, 3.4))
merged <- merge_norms(lex, aoa)
merged[merged$word %in% aoa$word, c("word", "frequency", "aoa")]
```

The join is case- and whitespace-insensitive on both sides, keeps the lexicon's
own row and column order, and refuses a norm column whose name already exists on
the lexicon. A silent rename would be the worst available outcome: it leaves the
dimension the design matches on under a name nothing looks for.

In a design you do not call this yourself. Name the tables in a `norms:` block and
the pipeline joins them before the pool is built, so a norm column can be filtered
on, matched on or spanned like any other dimension.

```yaml
norms:
  - path: norms/en_concreteness.csv
    join_on: word             # optional join key, default 'word'
    columns: [concreteness]   # optional; default every column but the key

pool_filters:
  concreteness: [2.0, 5.0]
match_on: [length, concreteness]
```

The join key is written `join_on`, because YAML reads a bare `on` as the boolean
true. A bare `on:` is read as the join key all the same, with a note in the run
log, and any other key in an entry is refused.

lexsync ships no norm data: licences vary, and the citation is yours to honour.
What it does do is record what you joined. Every table appears in the materials
datasheet with its checksum and its per-column coverage, because a norm table can
supply the very variable a design manipulates, and a selection over columns of
unstated origin is not reproducible from the record that exists to make it so.
Coverage is recorded for a related reason: a word the table does not cover gets a
missing value. A filter on the column drops it, and the matcher excludes it before
selecting whenever the column is a matched dimension, a continuous predictor or a
control. The run log and the datasheet count those exclusions per condition.

## Pool filters

A pool filter narrows the lexicon before any matching happens. It states what
counts as an eligible word at all, independently of condition, and it is the
right place for constraints you would apply to every item in the study.

```{r pool}
pool_filters <- list(length = c(3, 7), frequency = c(3.8, 7.0))
pool <- build_pool(lex, pool_filters)
c(lexicon = nrow(lex), pool = nrow(pool))
```

A numeric pair is read as an inclusive range. Any other vector is read as a set of
permitted values, so `list(pos = c("noun", "verb"))` would keep nouns and verbs
if the lexicon carried a `pos` column. Rows missing a value on a filtered column
are always dropped. Called directly, `build_pool()` skips a filter naming a column
the frame does not have, because it filters lexica, supplied pools and pair
tables, which carry different columns. A misspelt key passed to it directly
therefore silently widens the pool. The filters a design names are checked first.
`run_pipeline()` refuses a `pool_filters` key that names neither a column of the
lexicon, counting any columns its `norms:` tables add, nor a dimension the
pipeline derives (`n_density`, `old20` or `bigram_freq`), and `match_stimuli()`
refuses a `define_by` key the pool lacks, so a misspelt key in a design stops the
run.

Filtering is a separate step from matching. `match_stimuli()` reads a design's
`conditions` and `match_on` fields but never its `pool_filters`, so passing a raw
lexicon where a pool was intended silently widens the selection, with no error to
warn you. The pipeline calls `build_pool()` first and the examples here do the
same.

## Choosing and screening a lexicon

The lexica in the repository's `corpora/derived/` hold the most frequent forms
wordfreq gives for a language, and wordfreq lists names, acronyms and internet
forms beside words. Such forms enter a selection unevenly across conditions: when
the `en_andrews_repro` demonstration read `en.csv`, they made up 24 of its 36
low-frequency items and none of its 36 high-frequency ones. N and OLD20 count
them as neighbours too, so that `cat` has 32 neighbours in `en.csv`, among them
`caa`, `cbt` and `cdt`.

`corpora/derived/en_v2.csv` screens the English lexicon against SUBTLEX-US
(Brysbaert & New, 2009). It holds the 30,000 forms and frequencies of `en.csv`
and adds four columns. `in_subtlex_us` is 1 when SUBTLEX-US lists the form, and
`lowercase_share` is the share of its SUBTLEX-US uses that begin with a
lower-case letter, empty for a form SUBTLEX-US lacks. `nonstandard` is 1 for a
form SUBTLEX-US lacks or whose share is below 0.10, which marks 6,565 forms,
mostly names and acronyms, and `reference_member` is 1 for the other 23,435. The
file's `n_density` and `old20` count neighbours among those only, so `cat` has
21, and `n_density_raw` and `old20_raw` keep the values of `en.csv`. To select
among the unmarked forms, filter on the flag.

```yaml
lexicon: corpora/derived/en_v2.csv
pool_filters:
  nonstandard: [0, 0]
```

The threshold is low on purpose. A capital at the start of a sentence pulls
ordinary words down, so even `what`, `how`, `why`, `maybe`, `okay` and `yes`
begin with a lower-case letter in under half their uses. A filter such as
`lowercase_share: [0.5, 1]` would drop them all. Even at 0.10 the flag marks the
days of the week, the months other than `march` and `may`, most nationality
words, `god`, `ok` and `tv`. It also marks every form the 2009 corpus lacks,
such as `selfie`, `emoji` and `covid`. A design that needs some of those can
leave the flag unfiltered and remove what it does not want by name. A range
filter on `lowercase_share` would also drop every form SUBTLEX-US lacks, whose
share is empty.

`exclude_words` removes words by name. It lists them in the design, or names a
UTF-8 file with one word per line, in which blank lines and lines beginning `#`
are skipped.

```yaml
exclude_words: [adams, dubai, espn]
# or, from a file: exclude_words: {path: config/exclude_en.txt}
```

The words are trimmed, lower-cased and put in NFC, as a lexicon's words are.
They leave the candidates of a corpus, pool or generated design after any
`norms:` join and before the pool filters. The neighbourhood reference still
counts them, and a generated pseudoword still may not equal one, because an
excluded word is still a word of the language. A design with an item table
refuses the key, since its items are already a selection of your own. The
datasheet records the list as `materials_source$exclusions`, with its checksum,
the number of words it lists and the number of candidates it removed, and the
Methods paragraph reports the removal.

`en.csv` keeps its bytes, so a design written for lexsync 0.1 selects what it
selected once it sets `matching.tie_break: bytes` (see [Ties between equally close
candidates](#ties-between-equally-close-candidates) below), unless it uses the
`optimal` method, whose selections differ from those of lexsync 0.1 under either
rule, or its pool holds candidates that lack a matched value, which are now left
out. The English demonstrations read `en_v2.csv` with the filter above.
Their `exclude_words` file, `config/exclude_en_demo.txt`, leaves out the taboo
words and the forms that pass the screen without being standard English words,
such as abbreviations that subtitles write in lower case (`mph`, `msg`). Its
header states the criteria, and the list was made by reading what the
demonstrations selected. Spanish and Chinese have no screened lexicon, because no
source of letter case or known words with a verified licence exists for them.
Read a selection in either language before a study runs, and leave out what you
find with `exclude_words`.

The datasheet credits the lexicon a corpus or generated design read. A lexicon
lexsync ships is credited to wordfreq, and `en_v2.csv` and the English example
slice drawn from it to wordfreq screened against SUBTLEX-US, with the rule. A
corpus that `fetch_corpus()` put in the cache is credited by the registry's
citation, and any other file by its name and the first twelve digits of its
checksum.

## Supplied item pools

Narrowing a whole lexicon is the right way round when any word of the language
will do. It is the wrong way round when the candidate set is itself a research
decision: a list from a previous study, from a norming session, or one restricted
to a semantic category that no lexical filter can express. Loaded as a lexicon,
such a list would need an invented `freq_zipf` column, and, given as
`items.source: table`, it would skip matching.

`items.source: pool` takes the list as it is.

```yaml
items:
  source: pool
  path: items/pool_en_concrete_nouns.csv
  lexicon: corpora/derived/en_v2.csv
```

The list needs only a `word` column. Length and the syllable estimate are derived
from the form, and `items.lexicon` supplies the rest, frequency above all, by
lookup. A word the lexicon does not have raises a hard error, because the
tolerance windows drop rows with missing values silently and the pool would then
be smaller than it appears to be.

One subtlety would quietly invalidate the controls if it went the other way.
`n_density` and `old20` are properties of a word in its *language*, not among the
131 words of a supplied list, so they are computed against the lexicon's words. A
supplied pool with no lexicon falls back to itself, which is why one is given
above. `load_pool()` returns both parts of that, the pool and the reference word
list, if you call it directly outside a design.

Everything downstream is unchanged: the same conditions, the same `match_on`, the
same report, the same datasheet. What differs is only where the candidates came
from, and the datasheet records the list's checksum so that stays answerable
later. `design_en_supplied_pool.yaml` is a worked example.

## Relational designs, where the item is a pair

A priming study's theoretical variable is a property of the *pair*, such as
distributional similarity or associative strength, while its nuisance variables
are properties of each *member*: frequency, length, neighbourhood. A relational
design therefore needs matching and its own item table at once.

`items.members` promotes an ordinary item table to a pair-keyed one.

```yaml
items:
  source: table
  path: items/priming_pairs_en.csv
  members: [prime, target]             # the two word fields
  lexicon: corpora/derived/en_v2.csv   # where each member's norms are looked up
  anchor_condition: related            # whose row represents the pair during selection
```

Each member's word-level norms are joined from the lexicon and prefixed, giving
`prime.frequency`, `target.length` and so on. The member name leads and the
dimension follows, for a reason specific to R: `prime.frequency` is safe because
`df$prime` still exact-matches the bare `prime` column, whereas
`frequency.prime` would be a partial-matching hazard. Those prefixed names are
usable wherever a dimension is: in `pool_filters`, in `match_on`, as a
`continuous` predictor or as a control.

`pair.lev` is the Levenshtein distance between the two members and `pair.overlap`
is `1 - pair.lev / length of the longer form`, a normalised orthographic
similarity. It scores edit operations, so it is not a count of shared material:
`abc` and `cba` share every letter but score 0.33. Orthographic overlap is the
standard confound control in a priming design, since a related pair that also
shares letters confounds semantic relatedness with orthographic similarity. The
pipeline adds both automatically when the two members are named `prime` and
`target`. Under any other member names, call `add_pair_overlap()` on the item
table yourself. A predictor that cannot be computed from the forms alone, such as
cosine similarity or forward associative strength, arrives as an extra column on
the item table and is used like any other.

```yaml
n_per_condition: 8                  # counts PAIRS: 8 pairs, 16 rows, 8 per list
pool_filters:
  target.length: [3, 7]
  target.frequency: [3.0, 6.0]
continuous:
  predictor: target.frequency
  controls: [target.length, pair.overlap]
match_on: [target.length, pair.overlap]
```

Two rules follow from the item being a pair. A filter applies to a pair only if
*every* one of its rows passes, and selection runs over one row per pair, the
`anchor_condition`, defaulting to the byte-first condition, with the result
re-expanded afterwards so every condition row of every chosen pair survives.
Neither is an optimisation. A filter on `prime.frequency` applied row by row would
keep a pair's related row and drop its unrelated one, leaving a set the
Latin-square counterbalancer cannot complete. Only a dimension that varies within
the pair can split it that way, which the prime-level and pair-level ones do and
the target-level ones do not, since the target is the same word in both rows.

A member name may not be one of `word`, `id`, `set`, `list`, `trial`, `condition`,
`replicate` or `item`, which the engines read directly, and a design using one is
refused. The datasheet gains a `relational` block recording the members, the pair
count, the member lexicon and its checksum, and the member-level dimensions
separately from the relational ones. `design_en_priming_continuous.yaml` is the
worked example, and its own comments go further into why each rule is there.

## Conditions, the anchor and matched sets

A condition is a named region of the pool, given by `define_by`, which is read
exactly as `pool_filters` is. The first condition listed is the anchor. Its items
are chosen by an even spread across the sorted candidate subpool, so the anchor
covers the whole of its region on the manipulated dimension and does not cluster
at one end. Every later condition is then matched to the anchor item by item, and
the `set` column records the pairing. The matching needs at least one dimension in
`match_on`. Without one, every candidate lies at distance zero from every anchor
and the tie-break alone would choose the words, so a design with
conditions and no `match_on`, or an empty one, is refused before anything is
selected.

```{r design}
design <- list(
  name = "vignette_matching", language = "english", n_per_condition = 20,
  pool_filters = pool_filters,
  conditions = list(
    list(name = "high", define_by = list(frequency = c(5.2, 7.0))),
    list(name = "low",  define_by = list(frequency = c(3.8, 4.4)))
  ),
  match_on = list("length", "n_density", "old20")
)
stim <- match_stimuli(pool, design, schema)
head(
  stim[
    stim$set %in% 1:3,
    c("set", "condition", "word", "frequency", "length", "old20")
  ],
  6
)
```

Because the anchor is spread across its own subpool, the order of the conditions
is a design decision with consequences. The anchor's distribution on the
manipulated dimension is inherited from the pool, and every other condition's
distribution is whatever matching to that anchor produces.

## The four matching methods

The method is set with `matching.method` in a design, or left to the schema
default. All four minimise a distance in standardised space, computed by
z-scoring each `match_on` dimension against the whole pool, so that a letter and a
Zipf unit become comparable. They differ in what they minimise it over. A
candidate missing any `match_on` dimension has no place in that space, so every
method starts from the rows complete on all of them. The run log and the
datasheet count what each condition lost.

`standardised_euclidean`, the default, walks the anchor items in order and gives
each one its nearest unused counterpart, greedily. Because the anchor is selected
before any matching happens, it preserves the anchor's even spread exactly. Being
anchored, it generalises past two conditions, as `mahalanobis` does, while `joint`
and `optimal` score cross-condition pairs and are refused with any number of
conditions but two.

`joint` abandons the anchor. It scores every cross-condition pair, then takes the
best-matched pairs in ascending order of distance until it has enough, so an item
with no good counterpart is simply never selected. This equates the controls more
tightly than per-anchor matching when the manipulation is confounded with a
control, and the price is that the manipulated dimension's realised distribution
is no longer under your control. It requires exactly two conditions.

`mahalanobis` replaces the Euclidean metric with one weighted by the inverse of
the pool's correlation matrix, so that dimensions sharing variance are not
counted twice. It suits the case where the matched dimensions are strongly
intercorrelated, which is the normal case for orthographic measures. The
correlations come from the pool's rows that are complete on every matched
dimension, and with *k* matched dimensions the pool needs at least *k* + 2 such
rows.

```{r correlations}
round(cor(pool[, c("length", "n_density", "old20")]), 2)
```

Length, neighbourhood density and OLD20 are far from independent here. Under a
plain Euclidean metric, matching on all three counts the shared
length-neighbourhood variance three times over and lets an independent dimension
drift. Mahalanobis distance discounts that overlap (Rubin, 1980; Stuart, 2010).

`optimal` keeps the Euclidean metric and selects the *n* disjoint pairs whose
summed distance is smallest. Choosing *n* pairs from two pools is the
*k*-cardinality assignment problem, which lexsync solves exactly by padding the
cost matrix with dummy rows and columns until every optimal assignment uses
exactly *n* real pairs (Volgenant, 2004). Greedy matching can spend the one good
counterpart of a hard item on an easy item that had alternatives. Optimal
matching cannot, although on the pools tested `joint` came within a few per cent
of the optimum. Gu and Rosenbaum (1993) compared optimal and greedy pair matching
of every treated unit, a related problem, and found optimal matching no better
at balancing the covariates. When the conditions overlap, a word cannot be paired
with itself or used twice. A pair lost that way is replaced by solving again over
the unused words, and the selection is then no longer guaranteed to have the
least summed distance. The method requires exactly two conditions and the `clue`
package.

```{r methods}
methods <- c("standardised_euclidean", "joint", "mahalanobis")
if (requireNamespace("clue", quietly = TRUE)) methods <- c(methods, "optimal")

summarise_method <- function(method) {
  d <- design
  d$matching <- list(method = method)
  s <- match_stimuli(pool, d, schema)
  cmp <- match_report(
    s, c("frequency", "length", "n_density", "old20"), schema
  )$comparisons
  controls <- cmp[cmp$dimension != "frequency", ]
  high <- s$frequency[s$condition == "high"]
  low  <- s$frequency[s$condition == "low"]
  data.frame(
    method = method,
    worst_control_d = round(max(abs(controls$cohens_d)), 3),
    freq_d = round(cmp$cohens_d[cmp$dimension == "frequency"], 2),
    freq_raw_diff = round(mean(high) - mean(low), 2),
    freq_sd_high = round(sd(high), 2)
  )
}
do.call(rbind, lapply(methods, summarise_method))
```

The comparison rewards a careful reading, and it is a good illustration of why a
standardised difference should not be read as an effect size on its own. The two
pairing methods drive the control differences to zero, because a free choice
over all pairs can find counterparts that match exactly on all three dimensions.
The pool holds far more exact matches than the design needs, so each method's
rule for choosing among them decides the rest. `joint` takes them in tie-break
order, and those pairs turn out to cluster in frequency: its standardised
frequency separation is the largest of the four, yet its raw separation in Zipf
units is the smallest. Both facts have one cause, the clustering, which shrinks
the SD of the high condition and so shrinks the pooled SD that `freq_d` divides
by. A narrower manipulation can raise `d`. `optimal` finds pairs just as exact,
but its assignment solver chooses among them by its own internal order, and here
the high condition keeps more of its spread.

Whether that is a gain depends on the study. The anchor methods keep the high
condition spread across its whole band by construction, which supports a claim
about the band rather than about a cluster inside it, and it is variance you may
want if the manipulation is later modelled as continuous. The pairing methods
guarantee exact control of the nuisance dimensions where the pool allows it, but
how much of the band they keep depends on which of the exact matches they take.
These numbers describe this pool and this design. The point is how to make the
comparison, not which method wins.

### The parity caveat on two methods

The R and Python engines select byte-identical stimuli under
`standardised_euclidean` and `joint`. They do not guarantee it under
`mahalanobis` or `optimal`. Both of the latter route the distance through an
operation whose last bits are decided by the platform's linear-algebra
implementation, a covariance-matrix inverse in one case and an assignment solver
in the other, and once two candidate distances differ in their final bits the
tie-break that would otherwise make the engines agree never fires. `mahalanobis`
usually still agrees exactly, and `optimal` often selects an equally-optimal but
different set. Each run's datasheet records which case applies, under
`selection.cross_engine`. If cross-engine reproducibility is a requirement of
your project, `standardised_euclidean` and `joint` are the methods that carry the
guarantee. The
reproducibility vignette sets out why the exception cannot simply be engineered
away.

### Ties between equally close candidates

Lengths and neighbourhood counts are whole numbers and frequencies carry two
decimals, so candidates often lie at exactly the same distance from an anchor.
When `en_freqcontrast` read the unscreened English corpus, `en.csv`, 71 of its 80
anchored picks had another candidate at the chosen distance, and the tie-break
chose the word. `matching.tie_break` sets the rule, in a design or in the schema.
Under `bytes`, the rule of lexsync 0.1, a tie goes to the word whose UTF-8 bytes
sort first, and then to the lower id, so a condition decided by ties fills with
early-alphabet words. Under that rule, 61% of the design's low-frequency words
began with a or b, against 13% of their candidates. A word's initial phoneme
biases voice-key measures of naming latency (Kessler et al., 2002), and the
realised-control report cannot show such a skew, because it measures only the
matched dimensions.

Under `hash`, the default, a tie goes to the smaller SHA-256 digest of
`lexsync-tie-v1|` followed by the word. The salt is fixed, so the rule does not
depend on the seed, and the digests favour no part of the alphabet. The same rule
orders the tied pairs of `joint` and `optimal` and the rows tied at their
candidate cap.

```{r ties}
initial_share <- function(words) mean(substr(words, 1L, 1L) %in% c("a", "b"))
by_rule <- lapply(c(bytes = "bytes", hash = "hash"), function(rule) {
  d <- design
  d$matching <- list(tie_break = rule)
  match_stimuli(pool, d, schema)
})
low_candidates <- build_pool(pool, design$conditions[[2]]$define_by)
round(c(vapply(by_rule, function(s) initial_share(s$word[s$condition == "low"]),
               numeric(1)),
        candidates = initial_share(low_candidates$word)), 2)
```

On this small pool, the share says little. With 20 items it moves by chance
under either rule, and here it falls below the candidates' share under `hash`.
The skew shows plainly at the size of a full lexicon, as the `en_freqcontrast`
figures above do. Only the picks that ties decided can change, and here the
matched differences do not move.

```{r ties-control}
sapply(by_rule, function(s) {
  cmp <- match_report(s, c("length", "n_density", "old20"), schema)$comparisons
  stats::setNames(round(cmp$cohens_d, 3), cmp$dimension)
})
```

Under either rule, `standardised_euclidean` and `joint` give the same selection
in the two engines, and `bytes` reproduces the selections of lexsync 0.1. The even
spreads that pick the anchor's items and a continuous design's items keep the
byte order under both rules.

## Tolerance windows

Matching by distance alone will always return the nearest available candidate,
however far away it is. The tolerance window is the guard against that. Before
the distance ranking, each later condition's candidates are filtered to those
lying within the anchor's mean plus or minus *k* standard deviations on every
matched dimension, with *k* set per dimension.

```{r tolerance}
str(schema$matching$tolerance_k)
```

Smaller *k* is stricter. The default of 2.0 on the orthographic dimensions is
permissive, admitting most of a normal distribution, and it is meant as a backstop
against a wild counterpart. The distance ranking within the window is what does
the work of control. A design tightens the window per dimension, and only the
named dimensions are overridden. A dimension the schema does not list takes *k* = 2.
The design's values are merged over the schema's by `modifyList()`. A `null` in
the schema is ignored, and a `null` in the design removes the schema's value for
that dimension, so either leaves *k* at 2.

The window belongs to the anchored path, so it is what `standardised_euclidean`
and `mahalanobis` apply. `joint` and `optimal` score cross-condition pairs
directly and never read `tolerance_k` at all, which is worth knowing before
tightening a window and finding the selection unmoved.

```{r tolerance-override}
tight <- design
tight$matching <- list(tolerance_k = list(old20 = 0.25))
tight_stim <- match_stimuli(pool, tight, schema, verbose = TRUE)
round(match_report(tight_stim, "old20", schema)$comparisons$cohens_d, 3)
```

There is a behaviour here that will bite you if you do not know it. If a window
leaves a condition with fewer candidates than there are anchor items, the matcher
neither fails nor returns a short set. It relaxes that condition's window and
carries on. Tightening the window past what the pool can supply therefore looks
exactly like a window that was never set, and under the default policy
`verbose = TRUE` is the only thing that tells you which happened.

```{r tolerance-relaxed}
too_tight <- design
too_tight$matching <- list(tolerance_k = list(old20 = 0.05))
relaxed_stim <- match_stimuli(pool, too_tight, schema, verbose = TRUE)
```

Two details of the relaxation matter. It is per condition and it is
all-or-nothing: the fallback drops that condition's windows on *every* matched
dimension at once, not merely the one that proved unsatisfiable, so an
over-tightened `old20` also discards the `length` and `n_density` windows for
that condition. And it does not degrade the match as much as you might fear,
because the distance ranking still runs over the whole subpool and still prefers
near counterparts. Only when the relaxed subpool is still too small does the
matcher stop, with an error naming the condition and the counts.

Both behaviours are policies, and the schema's `matching` block names them.
`on_insufficient_tolerance` governs the fallback just described. Its default of
`relax` keeps the behaviour above, while `error` makes the matcher refuse and say
so, which is the honest setting when the window is itself the criterion,
as it is when reproducing a published study's stated windows. `shortfall`
governs what happens when fewer sets than `n_per_condition` can be selected at
all, and it defaults to `error` deliberately, because a smaller set changes the
design that was planned. A design that can live with fewer sets says so with
`shortfall: allow`. The datasheet then records the items each condition holds,
and the methods paragraph states them beside the request. Either key may be
overridden under the design's own `matching:` block, exactly as `tolerance_k` was
overridden above.

Windows are the place to reproduce a published study's stated criteria. The
repository's `config/design_es_gender_repro.yaml` sets `tolerance_k` to `0.111...` for
`frequency`, the window of the mean plus or minus SD/9 that González Alonso et al.
(2025) used, and to 2 for `length`, the mean plus or minus 2 SD.

One asymmetry is worth knowing. Tolerance windows are derived from the anchor, so
they apply to the anchor-based methods, `standardised_euclidean` and
`mahalanobis`, and to continuous designs. `joint` and `optimal` never build an
anchor and never consult `tolerance_k`. Both instead cap each subpool to the 1200
candidates nearest the other condition's centroid before pairing, which bounds
the cost of scoring every pair.

## Continuous designs

A matched dichotomy is not the only way to study a graded property, and for a
property like frequency it is often not the best one. Splitting a continuum into
a high and a low band discards the variation within each band, spends statistical
power to do it, and leaves the estimate dependent on where the split was placed.
The selection can also manufacture its own artefacts: Liben-Nowell et al. (2019)
show that choosing a controlled subset from a large candidate set can produce an
apparent effect from a set where none exists, because the selection is itself a
search over the space of possible item sets. Kuperman (2015) makes the
constructive case, that a megastudy's variation can be used directly by sampling
across a predictor's range and modelling it.

A `continuous` block does that. Rather than conditions, it names one predictor to
span and the controls to hold still, and the two must agree with `match_on`.

```{r continuous}
cont_design <- list(
  name = "vignette_continuous", language = "english", n_per_condition = 60,
  pool_filters = pool_filters,
  continuous = list(
    predictor = "frequency",
    controls = c("length", "n_density", "old20")
  ),
  match_on = list("length", "n_density", "old20"),
  matching = list(
    tolerance_k = list(length = 1.5, n_density = 1.5, old20 = 1.5)
  )
)
cont <- select_continuous_stimuli(pool, cont_design, schema)
nrow(cont)
range(cont$frequency)
```

Selection runs in two passes. An even spread over the pool's ranks on the
predictor defines the control windows from its own distribution, the pool is
filtered to those windows, and a second even spread over the ranks of what
survives is the selection. Because the spread is over ranks and not values, the
selection follows the pool's distribution of the predictor. In the
`en_freqcontinuous` demonstration its quantiles lie within 0.06 of the pool's,
and 95% of the items fall in the lower half of the frequency range, since
frequent words are rare in any lexicon. The windows trim the controls' tails
without holding the controls constant, so how far each control is still
correlated with the predictor has to be read from the report.

```{r continuous-report}
cont_report <- match_report_continuous(
  cont, "frequency",
  c("length", "n_density", "old20"), schema
)
cont_report$comparisons
```

The report is read differently from a matched one. `predictor_span` is the
realised range of the predictor in the selected set and should be wide, since it
is the variation the regression has to work with. Each control's `pearson_r` is its correlation
with the predictor and should be near zero, since a control that still correlates
with the predictor is still a confound. Tightening `tolerance_k` does not reliably
lower those correlations. In `en_freqcontinuous`, k = 1.0 gives a correlation of
0.070 between frequency and `n_density`, against 0.301 at k = 1.5, but on the
unscreened `en.csv` it gave 0.213 against -0.049. At k = 0.25 only 30 items fall
within the windows, fewer than the 80 the design needs, so the selector relaxes
them to the whole pool. A control that stays correlated belongs in the model as a
covariate.

Each row also gives the dimension's realised SD as `sd`. For the predictor,
`sd_ratio` sets it against the SD of as many values spaced evenly over the same
range. That SD is `(max - min) * sqrt(n * (n + 1) / 12) / (n - 1)`, which
approaches `(max - min) / sqrt(12)` as n grows, so an even spread has a ratio of 1
at any size. A ratio below 1 means the items bunch together more than an even spread
would: `en_freqcontinuous` has 0.59, an SD of 0.53 against 0.90. A ratio above 1
means they gather towards the ends of the range. For a control, `sd_ratio` sets
the realised SD against the SD of the pool the selector drew from, and
`window_low` and `window_high` give the window its first pass set. In
`en_freqcontinuous`, length keeps 0.76 of the pool's SD, so the window trims the
tails of a control and leaves much of its spread. The windows come from the
`"audit"` attribute `select_continuous_stimuli()` attaches to its result, which
`match_report_continuous()` reads unless it is given one as `audit`. A window that
held too few items and was widened to the whole pool is recorded in the
datasheet's `window_relaxations`.

The datasheet for a continuous design reports the span, the correlations and a
suggested regression model in which the controls enter as covariates. Its methods
paragraph sets the predictor's SD against that of an even spread, gives each
control's window and its realised SD against the pool's, and says when the windows
were widened.

## Reading the realised control

`match_report()` returns two data frames. The descriptives give per-condition n,
mean, SD, minimum, median and maximum for each dimension, which is the table that
belongs in a paper's materials section.

```{r report-desc}
report <- match_report(
  stim, c("frequency", "length", "n_density", "old20"), schema
)
knitr::kable(
  report$descriptives,
  caption = "Descriptive statistics per condition"
)
```

The comparisons contrast every pair of conditions on every dimension. The rows
against the anchor come first, and every further pair follows in condition order,
with the earlier condition of the pair named in `reference`. A 2 x 2 design such
as `en_andrews_repro` therefore shows the contrasts within each factor, such as
its two low-frequency cells, beside the three against its first cell. The rows
carry the statistics that answer whether the matching worked.

```{r report-comp}
knitr::kable(
  report$comparisons,
  caption = paste(
    "Realised control: standardised differences with 90% intervals,",
    "variance ratios, TOST verdicts and raw differences"
  )
)
```

`cohens_d` is the standardised mean difference, using the pooled SD. It is the
mean of the condition named in `reference` minus the mean of the condition in that
row, so a positive d means the reference scores higher. It should be large on the
manipulated dimension and near zero on a controlled one. A condition with a single
item has no spread, so d and its interval are then `NA`.

`d_ci_low` and `d_ci_high` bound it with a 90% confidence interval, built from
the large-sample standard error of d (Hedges & Olkin, 1985). That standard error
grows with d itself, so the interval on a manipulated dimension is much wider
than on a well-matched control with the same number of items. The interval,
not the point estimate, is the primary summary of a controlled dimension. Its
upper limit is the largest imbalance still consistent with the stimuli you have,
and with few items that limit can be substantial even when the point estimate is
almost zero. Reporting the interval keeps the dependence on set size visible,
where a bare 'no significant difference' hides it.

`var_ratio` is the condition's variance over the reference's. Two conditions can
share a mean and still confound if one is far more spread out than the other,
which every mean-based statistic misses, so this is the distributional check. A
ratio near 1 is balanced and a common heuristic flags ratios outside roughly 0.5
to 2. See `?variance_ratio` for the sources behind that heuristic.

`mean_diff` is the same contrast in the dimension's own unit: the reference mean
minus the condition mean, in letters, Zipf units, neighbours or syllables, to
three places. It is defined whenever each condition has an item, so it remains
when d is `NA`.

`role` says what the design did with the dimension in that pair. A dimension is
`manipulated` when the two conditions' `define_by` windows on it differ,
`controlled` when the design matches on it, and `uncontrolled` otherwise. The
role belongs to the pair: in `en_andrews_repro`, frequency is manipulated between
a high- and a low-frequency cell and uncontrolled between the two high-frequency
cells, which share the window [5, 7]. `run_pipeline()` derives the roles from the
design and passes them to `match_report()` as `roles`, a function of the row's
condition, reference and dimension. Called without it, as above, `match_report()`
leaves `role` as `NA`.

The pipeline reports every dimension lexsync knows for the items, whether or not
the design matches on it. Length, frequency, N, OLD20, syllables and bigram
frequency come first, then the matched dimensions, every `define_by` dimension and
every joined norm column, so a norm that defines the conditions appears as the
manipulated dimension it is. Bigram frequency is computed for the report when the stimuli
lack it, which leaves the stimuli file and the selection as they were. A dimension
with no numeric value among the items, such as `n_syllables` for Chinese words, is
left out. The uncontrolled rows are where a confound shows. In `en_ndensity`, the
dense words have fewer estimated syllables than the sparse ones (d = -0.53, 90% CI
[-0.79, -0.26]), which a report of the matched dimensions alone could not reveal.

`tost_p` and `equivalent` are the two one-sided tests. A conventional
non-significant difference test is not evidence of equivalence, because failing
to reject a null is not the same as supporting it, and the failure is easiest to
achieve with few items and noisy measures. TOST inverts this by testing against
an explicit bound: the reported p is the larger of two one-sided p-values against
a difference of plus or minus `bound_d` pooled SDs, and a value below alpha
supports equivalence within that bound (Lakens, 2017). The bound and alpha are
the schema's, so the verdict is only as meaningful as the bound you chose.

```{r equivalence-settings}
str(schema$equivalence)
```

A bound of 0.5 SD is the schema default and it is a convention rather than a
finding. It is not a default of Lakens (2017), who asks for the bound to be
justified for the study at hand. Half a standard deviation is a permissive bound
for a nuisance dimension in a design where that dimension has a strong effect on
the response. A study that cares about a particular confound should set a bound
it can defend. The verdict also depends on the number of items: at a bound of 0.5
and an alpha of .05, no dimension that varies can pass with fewer than 23 items
per condition, even when the conditions are identical.

The 90% interval is the 1 - 2 x alpha interval so that it goes with the TOST
decision at alpha: the test
declares equivalence when the interval falls inside the bounds, and the interval
and the verdict are two readings of nearly the same thing. They are not quite
identical, because TOST tests the raw mean difference while the interval also
allows for the sampling error of the pooled SD. For a control near zero the two
agree to well within the published rounding. For a limit close to the bound,
`tost_p` is the verdict.

Both statistics treat the selected items as a sample from a larger population,
which they are not. Sassenhagen and Alday (2016) point out that a test on stimuli
concerns a closed population (the items you chose). They recommend describing the
stimuli, which the descriptives do, and entering potential confounds in the
analysis as covariates.

The datasheet's methods paragraph follows that advice. It describes the realised
control first: the largest difference on a matched dimension, in that dimension's
unit, with d and its interval. The interval is labelled by the schema's alpha, 90%
at .05 and 99% at .005. Raw differences in different units cannot be ranked against
each other, so the largest is the one with the largest |d|. The two one-sided tests come
second, as a check, with the number of matched comparisons they supported. When
every condition holds fewer items than the bound needs, the paragraph says that no
dimension that varies can pass, however well matched. It then names, largest first,
up to five comparisons of a dimension the design did not control whose |d| exceeds
the bound, such as the syllable difference in `en_ndensity`, or says that none
does. The suggested model enters the matched dimensions as centred covariates.

The individual statistics are exported and can be called directly on any two
vectors.

```{r direct-stats}
high <- stim$old20[stim$condition == "high"]
low  <- stim$old20[stim$condition == "low"]
str(cohens_d_ci(high, low))
str(tost_equiv(high, low, bound_d = 0.5))
round(variance_ratio(low, high), 3)
```

`balance_check()` is the last piece and answers a different question: whether the
levels of a column occur equally often. It returns human-readable warnings and an
empty vector when all is well, and the pipeline logs whatever it returns.

```{r balance}
balance_check(stim, "condition")
balance_check(rbind(stim, stim[1, ]), "condition")
```

## Pseudowords

Lexical decision needs non-words, and the difficulty is that they must be
orthographically plausible without being real. `build_lexdec_stimuli()` draws real
words by an even spread across the byte-ordered pool, then generates a
length-matched pseudoword for each.

```{r lexdec}
lexdec_pool <- build_pool(lex, list(length = c(4, 7), frequency = c(3.5, 6.0)))
stim_lexdec <- build_lexdec_stimuli(
  lexdec_pool, n = 8, reference_words = lex$word
)
head(stim_lexdec[, c("target", "condition", "length", "set")], 4)
```

The presented string is `target`, the conditions are `word` and `pseudoword`, and
`set` pairs each word with its non-word twin. `reference_words` should be the full
lexicon: it supplies the bigram statistics and the list of real forms a pseudoword
must avoid, and it defaults to the pool when omitted, which is rarely what you
want.

Two methods are available, chosen per design under `items.generation.method`.

`letter_substitution`, the default, changes as few letters as possible subject to
three constraints: every resulting bigram must be attested in the corpus, the form
must not be in the reference list or already generated, and the length must be
preserved exactly. Single substitutions are searched first, then pairs as a
fallback. Among the legal candidates the most bigram-typical wins, with a
byte-order tie-break.

`subsyllabic` splits each word into onset, nucleus and coda constituents and swaps
whole constituents for attested alternatives of the same role and length, so the
pseudowords keep their syllabic structure. Codas and nuclei are changed before
onsets, which carry the most identifying orthography. Up to ceil(2k/3) of a
word's k constituents are replaced, each swap preserves length, and a word with
no legal swap falls back to letter substitution, so every word yields a
pseudoword. It is a deterministic orthographic approximation of Wuggy (Keuleers
& Brysbaert, 2010), and it differs from Wuggy in more than the phonological
model. Wuggy matches the template's transition frequencies, matches letter length
by default and has orthographic modules for several languages, and by default it
keeps two thirds of the segments where lexsync replaces up to two thirds. What
lexsync gains is cross-engine reproducibility.

```{r subsyllabic}
sub_stim <- build_lexdec_stimuli(
  lexdec_pool, n = 8, reference_words = lex$word, method = "subsyllabic"
)
# The real words come first in the frame, so pair each with its twin by `set`.
merge(
  sub_stim[sub_stim$condition == "word", c("set", "target")],
  sub_stim[sub_stim$condition == "pseudoword", c("set", "target")],
  by = "set", suffixes = c("_word", "_pseudoword")
)[1:4, ]
```

In both methods, the scoring picks the most bigram-typical candidate and does not
match the base word, so the pseudowords come out more bigram-typical than their
words. The difference in mean bigram probability is about d = -1.0, words minus
pseudowords, in `en_lexdec` and `en_lexdec_wuggy` alike. Read the generated forms
before a study runs.

Both generators process base words in byte order, so the set of already-used
pseudowords evolves identically in the two engines and both select byte-identical
stimuli. Their alphabet is derived from the reference. It is the set of letters the
reference words attest, in UTF-8 byte order, so a Spanish lexicon lends them `á`,
`é`, `í`, `ó`, `ú`, `ü` and `ñ`, which one word in six carries in a typical Spanish
band.
`build_lexdec_stimuli()` keeps the pool's words written wholly in those letters,
and a generated design's datasheet counts these words in the band as its
candidates. A word with a hyphen, an apostrophe or a digit is left out. The
subsyllabic segmenter takes its nuclei from the vowels of the syllable estimate,
whatever their accent, and a word without one, such as a Russian or Greek word,
goes down the letter-substitution path. Chinese is refused, since Unicode counts
its characters as letters but a form made by swapping one character for another
is of unknown validity as a pseudoword. In the Spanish demonstration,
`design_es_lexdec.yaml`, 8 of the 60 words and 4 of the pseudowords hold a letter
outside a to z, and the pseudowords are checked against wordfreq's Spanish word
list.

The stimuli give each pseudoword its `base` word and its `edit_distance` from it,
the Levenshtein distance, and give a word its own form and 0. A generated design's
report compares the words with their pseudowords on length, which they share by
construction, and on bigram frequency, N and OLD20, which the generator does not
hold. The report marks length as controlled and the other three as uncontrolled,
and it computes those three against the lexicon on a copy of the stimuli. Since
the most bigram-plausible candidate wins, the pseudowords tend to be more
bigram-typical than their words: in `en_lexdec` the difference is d = -0.97 (90%
CI [-1.29, -0.65]).

A pseudoword is a non-word only relative to the reference words, so a real word
too rare for the lexicon can still come out as one. The bundled English and
Spanish lexica stop at Zipf 2.95 and 3.11, and with the English lexicon alone the
generators can produce real words such as crier and pall. `exclude` names further
known word forms that no pseudoword may equal. They are trimmed, lower-cased and
put in NFC like the lexicon's words, and they take no part in the bigram
statistics. In a design the list goes under `items.generation.exclude`, and each
entry is a file with one form per line, a CSV file with a `word` column, or a
registry corpus already fetched into the cache:

```yaml
items:
  source: generate
  lexicon: corpora/derived/en_v2.csv
  generation:
    exclude: [corpora/derived/en_known_forms.txt]
```

Each file must be UTF-8 text, and no form in a one-form-per-line file may hold a
tab, a comma or a semicolon. Such a file is a table whose rows would each be kept
whole as a form that matches nothing, so it is refused. The datasheet records
each list with its checksum and the number of forms it holds, and the Methods
paragraph names it. In the lexsync repository,
`python corpora/fetch_corpora.py --known-forms en es` writes wordfreq's fuller
lists to `corpora/derived/` (289,023 English and 334,625 Spanish forms at Zipf 1.0
or above). They are not shipped in the package.

A long list costs the pseudowords some of their form. The generators' only check
on form is that each letter pair occurs somewhere in the lexicon, so with fewer
candidates left the most bigram-typical one can be ill-formed. In the English
demonstrations, 13 of the 140 pseudowords are ill-formed, among them fdes, gngs
and ntena. Each lacks a vowel or opens or closes on a letter pair that opens or
closes no screened English word of three letters or more with a vowel. Without
the list, the same designs give 5 such pseudowords. Read the generated forms
before a study runs.

`generate_pseudowords()` and `make_pseudoword()` are available directly if you
want the forms without the lexical-decision scaffolding around them.

```{r pseudowords}
generate_pseudowords(c("house", "table"), lex$word)
```

In a design this is `items.source: generate`, with the method under
`items.generation.method`. `design_en_lexdec.yaml` and `design_en_lexdec_wuggy.yaml`
are the worked examples of the two methods, and `design_en_lexdec_blocks.yaml`
adds practice and filler blocks to the same generated set.

## Items as a random factor

A matched set is one sample from the language, and an analysis that treats its
items as fixed generalises to those items rather than to the language they were
drawn from (Clark, 1973; Yarkoni, 2022). Crossed random effects are the standard
answer, and the datasheet suggests a model that includes them. `resample_stimuli()`
supports the stronger move of drawing several fully matched sets that share no
items, each one an independent sample, which lets a study run different item
samples across participant groups or show that an effect survives the change of
materials.

```{r resample}
reps <- resample_stimuli(pool, design, schema, n_sets = 2)
table(reps$replicate, reps$condition)
length(intersect(
  reps$word[reps$replicate == 1],
  reps$word[reps$replicate == 2]
))
```

Each replicate is matched independently against the pool with the earlier
replicates' items removed, so the sets are disjoint by construction. Later
replicates draw from a depleted pool, which means match quality can degrade
across replicates. The report will show it if it does.
